articles.title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11317-6De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
articles.content: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1–5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6–8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in designing artificial metalloenzymes via de novo protein design and directed evolution, enabling highly enantioselective photocatalysis. This advancement has broad implications for asymmetric catalysis, a key process in chemical synthesis, potentially improving efficiency and sustainability in pharmaceutical and chemical manufacturing. The study provides detailed context about the methodology and impact, indicating a meaningful and tangible benefit to science and industry.

articles.personality_presentation:

One way to do this is using special proteins combined with metals, called artificial metalloenzymes, but finding the right protein shapes has been slow and difficult.

**What happened** – Researchers used computer design to build new protein shapes from scratch that can hold metal catalysts used in light-powered reactions. They then improved these proteins through a method called directed evolution, which mimics natural selection to make them work better. These new proteins help the metal catalysts work faster and more precisely, controlling the exact shape of the molecules made.

**Impact** – This is the first time scientists have designed completely new proteins that help metal catalysts carry out light-driven reactions with high control over molecule shapes. It means chemists can now create better catalysts for making complex chemicals, including medicines, in a cleaner and more efficient way. The proteins also help recycle the catalysts, making the process more sustainable.

**What's next step** – The team will likely explore using these new protein-metal helpers for different chemical reactions and test how well they work in real-world manufacturing. This approach could lead to new tools for chemists to design custom catalysts for many purposes.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New computer-designed proteins combined with metals improve light-driven chemical reactions by precisely controlling molecule shapes, offering better ways to make important chemicals.

articles.title: Digital scents could add a new dimension to virtual worlds
articles.summary: It's now possible to convert a handful of smells into electronic signals that can be sent through the internet
articles.content:
It's now possible to convert a handful of smells into electronic signals that can be sent through the internet

The familiar scent of orange can now be transmitted through the internet Counter/Getty Images

Imagine if, in addition to sharing photos of those muffins you just baked, you could share their delicious aroma, too. That’s the promise of an AI-assisted device that can transmit smells over the internet. So far, it works on only a small number of scents, including orange, beer and cake, but its creators hope the system will ultimately recreate more smells. The scent of a pine forest or the aroma of coffee, for example, could then add a new dimension to virtual worlds and long-distance communication.

Although it is now routine to communicate sight, sound and even touch sensations electronically, smell is “still a very undeveloped sense”, says Chunyu Yang at the Ohio State University. That’s partly because odours involve complex chemistry. Whereas vision, for example, can be broken down into combinations of red, green and blue pixels, says Yang, there’s no simple building block underlying smell. Any attempt to convert aromas into electronic signals has to recognise combinations of very different molecules.

To solve the problem, Yang and her colleagues built an electronic nose, or “e-nose”, as well as a smell generator, then used machine learning to connect the two. The e-nose consists of arrays of sensors made of metal oxide. When different gaseous components of smells, such as ethanol (from alcoholic drinks) or limonene (found in citrus fruits), bind to the sensors’ surface, this changes their resistance, creating different electrical signals.

Advertisement

The researchers then trained an AI algorithm to recognise the distinctive signals created by smells from five different foods or beverages: orange, cake, coffee, beer and red wine. Teaching the AI to correctly recognise the smells was “the most challenging part” of the entire study, says Yang, because to generate enough data to train the system, she had to expose the sensors to the various smells hundreds of times.

This information was then sent over the internet to a smell generation device that the researchers are calling “Scentronic”. This part of the system involves miniature containers holding liquids laced with each of the five smells. Above each container is an atomiser that vibrates in response to electric signals, forcing the liquid in the container through a cotton filter and releasing fine droplets into the air, creating the appropriate smell, or combination of smells.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter

Yang built several different designs including stringing the atomisers onto a necklace and a wristband, and mounting them on a handheld device. When she tested the handheld device on 14 volunteers, they correctly identified the smells being transmitted to them 73 per cent of the time, on average.

She also built a prototype that reproduces taste, involving a cup of water with electromagnetic pumps containing flavoured liquid fixed around its edge. “When it receives information from the internet, the corresponding liquid will be dropped into the cup.”

Alternative methods to generate smells remotely have been suggested, including heating wax to release particular scents, and even stimulating neurons directly to create the experience of smell. But Yang argues her method is both fast and practical. She now hopes to expand the repertoire of the system, to create more complex aromas.

She suggests the entertainment industry could be first to develop the technology, to create more immersive virtual worlds. But there could also be health applications. For instance, the smell of food transforms the eating experience, so the technology could be adapted to make soldiers’ or astronauts’ rations more palatable. The Scentronic system could also enable doctors to assess distortions in patients’ sense of smell, for example, in post-viral illness or neurodegenerative disease.

The Scentronic system is “a great idea” and a step in the right direction, says Marianna Obrist at University College London, although she points out that recognising a smell and then releasing a matching one from a limited library is very different from the ease with which we can transmit sound and vision. “There’s still a long way to go before we can truly record and replay smell experiences.”

articles.title: This is what the mysterious Denisovans looked like
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03360-0Archaeologists identified skull fragments from China as belonging to this group of ancient human relatives.
articles.content:
Artist depiction of the heavy set facial features of a Denisovan.Credit: Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology/Chinese Academy of Sciences

A low, sloping forehead, a massive brow ridge that curves backwards, rectangle-like eye sockets, flat cheeks, and a moderately elevated bridge of the nose. Taken together, these features are the hallmarks of the ancient humans called the Denisovans, say researchers who studied a trove of fossilized skull fragments, teeth and jaws found in northern China.

“We are finally starting to put a face to the Denisovan,” says Sally Wasef, a palaeogeneticist at the Queensland University of Technology in Brisbane, Australia.

Denisovans were first described in 2010, after researchers sequenced genetic material from a mysterious finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia and found that it did not resemble that of Homo sapiens or Neanderthals. Ancient proteins have since been used to identify remains from other parts of Asia as Denisovan, including the first near-complete Denisovan skull found near Harbin, which helped put a face on the ancient humans.

Researchers report in Nature1 today that they have an even better idea of what Denisovans looked like after analysing the physical features of remains that belong to a collection of 20 fossils found in Xujiayao.

The Xujiayao remains are at least 130,000 years old and were found in the 1970s, alongside animal remains and tools. At the time, it was unclear what type of human these fossils belonged to, and they were classified as a species called Homo juluensis. By analysing ancient proteins from some of the fossils, Qiaomei Fu, a geneticist at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing, and her team identified the remains as Denisovan.

Wasef says ancient protein analysis is a valuable tool to complement DNA studies, particularly because proteins can survive longer than can DNA without fully degrading. Although DNA provides more detailed information about an individual, protein analysis can still yield useful information about who an individual is related to.

Fabrice Demeter, a palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, says the findings add to growing evidence that Denisovans were a widespread and potentially diverse group of humans. “The study represents a major step forward” in our understanding of what these humans could have looked like and where they lived.

Face to the name

Fu’s team analysed small fragments of proteins, called peptides, from two Xujiayao bones and compared them with peptides found in humans and Neanderthals. They found a single amino-acid change that was present in multiple peptides from the Xujiayao bones and other East Asian fossils and is a known genetic marker for identifying Denisovans. The amino-acid change was not seen in human or Neanderthal samples.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in paleoanthropology through the use of ancient protein analysis to identify Denisovan fossils and reconstruct their physical appearance. This discovery advances our understanding of human evolution and ancient human relatives, which has broad scientific and educational significance.

Ils ont décrit leurs traits du visage, comme un front bas, un arc sourcilier fort, des orbites rectangulaires et des joues plates.

**Impact** – Cette étude donne la description la plus claire à ce jour des Denisoviens. Elle montre aussi qu’ils vivaient dans une zone plus large qu’on ne le pensait et qu’ils avaient probablement des apparences variées. L’analyse des protéines, en plus de l’ADN, aide à identifier les humains anciens même quand l’ADN est trop abîmé.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à utiliser l’analyse des protéines pour étudier plus de fossiles et mieux comprendre la répartition et la diversité des Denisoviens. Cela pourrait révéler davantage sur la vie et les interactions des humains anciens.

**Résumé en une phrase** – De nouvelles études sur des fossiles et des protéines ont permis aux scientifiques de voir enfin le visage des mystérieux Denisoviens, enrichissant notre connaissance des humains anciens.
